subject: aerial survey design from a central point

messages.author: 6de9a0534fa1c61b
messages.subject: aerial survey design from a central point
parts:
Hi everybody,

I am working in the gobi areas in Mongolia and will do an aerial survey =
this November. The plane we will be using is a Jabiru J-430. We have to =
fly out and back for refuel from one single airport roughly in the =
middle of the survey area. The maximum distance we can cover with the =
plane before we need to refuel is 600km. The total area we want to cover =
is ~100,000 km=B2 and we have a maximum of 14 days for the survey. We =
will be counting Asiatic wild ass and if possible also goithered and =
Mongolian gazelles. So much for a background.

Now I am struggling with an intelligent survey design that allows us to =
cover the large area most efficiently. Intuitively I come up with flying =
like "the spikes of a wheel" type survey. This would oversample the =
middle and undersample the margins (almost like a trapping grid). I =
tried other geometrical designs but at some point decided that other =
people probably have run into the same problem before and most likely =
came up with an inteligent design.

By the way, has anybody used a Jabiru J-430 for a survey? Any advise =
about using this particular plane typ?

Can somebody help, rather quickly? Please see my contact details below. =
Best regards,
Petra

messages.author: 4b4a7b00c1dd09c7
messages.subject: Re: aerial survey design from a central point
parts:
Hi Petra, list,

Interesting problem. I don't have anything to contribute about the plane,
but here are some thoughts about the study design.

You're quite right that a spoke design will oversample the middle and
undersample the edge. It is relatively easy to work out what the coverage
probability will be for each point in your survey area under this design,
and methods exist for obtining an unbiased estimate of density/abundance
with uneven coverage designs if one knows the coverage probability (see
Advanced Distance Sampling book section 7.3). At St Andrews, we are
actually working on a project at present to create some uneven coverage
design classes (in our case where more effort is directed to areas thought
to contain more animals) and bundle that into Distance. We could
potentially add the spoke design in to this effort, so at some point in the
future the analysis could be done in Distance. We're therefore potentially
interested in collaborating on this -- feel free to contact me off the list
to discuss further.

A standard, equal coverage design, like a set of systematic parallel lines
spanning the study area, would however be easier to analyze. Another
advantage is that pooling robustness (see Intro book section 2.3.1, advances
book section 11.12) operates for even coverage designs, but not for uneven
ones. However, you'd have to contend with *lots* of off-effort time, so the
results may have higher variance. Depends to some extent on the
distribution of animals -- if there are lots of animals at the boundaries of
the study area then the spokes design, where there is low coverage out
there, is going to lead to high variances even though there is more on-
effort time.

If you did the systematic parallel lines design, you could also survey
during the "off-effort" periods and then do two analyses: one using just the
designed, "on-effort" stuff in a simple design based analysis, and one using
both on effort and off effort data using density surface modelling methods
(advanced book chapter 4). Density surface modelling methods are being
incorporated into Distance and should be available in a public beta version
quite soon.

A colleague here wondered whether wild asses are quite rare, so whether
you'll actually see enough of them in 14 days to do something useful with
(like fit a detection function). But I assume you've considered that.

Cheers,

- Len

messages.author: f2b64d27814968e8
messages.subject: Re: aerial survey design from a central point
parts:
=20
Hello

My experience with aerial survey off coastal Iceland, where there is a =
similar shortage of airfields that have the right fuel, leads me to =
suggest that it is better not to pay too much attention to this in the =
survey design. What I mean by this is that it is better to concentrate =
on achieving an unbiased design, with even coverage within strata, and =
to stratify your effort with regard to expected density if you have any =
prior knowledge of it. In this way your estimates will be unbiased and =
as precise as you can make them with the given amount of effort.

What you may find, as I did, is that the problem of wasted ferrying time =
solves itself. You can usually follow a transect out to an area, survey =
in that area until your endurance limit is near, then follow another =
transect back towards base. This requires careful flight planning and =
good cooperation with the pilot, and the ability to change the plan in =
mid-flight if that becomes necessary because of weather or other =
factors.=20

Of course all this depends on the size and shape of the area, and the =
stratification scheme used. But again my suggestion would be to give =
first priority to achieving an unbiased design, and then use flight =
planning and strategy to optimize the use of the plane.=20

I hope your survey goes well!
